lead: An infinite series adds infinitely many real numbers: a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + … . You cannot finish the addition, so the sum is defined as a limit. Add the first N terms to get the partial sum S_N. If the sequence S_N converges to a real number S, the series converges and S is its sum. Otherwise it diverges. This turns every series question into a sequence question from 3.1. Series are used in payment plans with interest, function approximations, and sampled signals.
prereq: You need 3.1 for the limit of a sequence and the notation aₙ → L.

blocks.text: A series of real numbers is a sum with infinitely many terms: Σ_{n=1}∞ aₙ = a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + … . Each aₙ is a real number called a term. The N-th partial sum is S_N = a₁ + a₂ + … + a_N. This is an ordinary finite sum. The sequence of partial sums is S₁, S₂, S₃, … . The series converges to a real number S when lim_{N→∞} S_N = S. Then we write Σ_{n=1}∞ aₙ = S. If the limit does not exist as a finite real number, the series diverges. Some syllabi stress the sequence of partial sums; the convergence of that sequence is what defines the sum of the series.
Infinite addition has no last term, so the limit supplies the missing meaning. A series is not a number until its partial sums settle. If S_N alternates between 0 and 1, the series diverges.
Σ_{n=1}∞ aₙ = lim_{N→∞} S_N, where S_N = a₁ + a₂ + … + a_N
blocks.where: aₙ are the terms; S_N is the N-th partial sum; S is the sum when the limit exists.

blocks.text: Every convergence question about a series is a convergence question about the sequence S_N from 3.1. Whether aₙ tends to 0 alone does not decide it. The convergence question is decided by the partial sums S_N.

A geometric series has each term r times the previous term. The first term is a and the common ratio is r. Then Σ_{n=1}∞ a r^{n−1} = a + ar + ar² + … . For r ≠ 1, S_N = a(1 − r^N)/(1 − r). If |r| < 1, then r^N → 0, so S_N → a/(1 − r). The series converges and its sum is a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, it diverges, except the zero series with a = 0. The first term a carries the unit; r is a pure number.

In a telescoping series, each term splits as a difference bₙ − b_{n+1}. Then S_N = (b₁ − b₂) + (b₂ − b₃) + … + (b_N − b_{N+1}) = b₁ − b_{N+1}. The middle terms cancel. If b_{N+1} → L, the sum is b₁ − L. The worked example uses bₙ = 1/n.

sections.h3: The nth term test and algebra

blocks.text: The nth term test. If Σaₙ converges, then aₙ → 0. Reason: aₙ = S_n − S_{n−1}, and both partial sums tend to the same S, so their difference tends to 0. Contrapositive: if aₙ does not tend to 0, the series diverges. This test can prove divergence only. It cannot prove convergence. The harmonic series has aₙ = 1/n → 0 but diverges.

Algebra of convergent series. If Σaₙ = A and Σbₙ = B, both finite, then Σ(aₙ + bₙ) = A + B and Σ c aₙ = cA for any real constant c. Also Σ(aₙ − bₙ) = A − B. If Σaₙ converges and Σbₙ diverges, then Σ(aₙ + bₙ) diverges. Otherwise subtracting the convergent series would make Σbₙ converge. Adding or removing finitely many initial terms changes the sum but not convergence. For deeper tests see 3.3.
Σ(aₙ + bₙ) = Σaₙ + Σbₙ,   Σ c aₙ = c Σaₙ
blocks.where: valid when both series on the right converge; c is a real constant.

sections.h3: Cauchy criterion and the harmonic series

blocks.text: Cauchy criterion for series. The series Σaₙ converges if and only if for every ε > 0 there is an integer N such that for all m > n ≥ N, |a_{n+1} + a_{n+2} + … + a_m| < ε. Here ε is any positive tolerance. The sum inside is a tail block of consecutive terms. This is exactly the Cauchy criterion for the partial sums S_N. The real line is complete, so a Cauchy sequence of partial sums has a real limit; see 3.8.

Harmonic series. Σ_{n=1}∞ 1/n diverges. Group terms after the first 1 and 1/2: 1 + 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) + (1/5 + … + 1/8) + … . For k ≥ 1, the block from 1/(2^k + 1) to 1/2^{k+1} has 2^k terms, each at least 1/2^{k+1}. The terms 1 and 1/2 stand outside the blocks. So each block sums to at least 2^k · 1/2^{k+1} = 1/2. Infinitely many blocks make partial sums larger than any bound. Thus S_N → ∞ and the series diverges. The integral comparison in 3.3 gives the same result through log N.

blocks.where: each bracket after the first two terms has sum at least 1/2; the brackets continue forever.

figure.caption: Terms form the partial sums S_N. The series has a sum only on the branch where S_N has a finite limit S.

spec.title: From terms to sum
spec.aria: The flow shows terms forming partial sums, and the series converges only when those partial sums have a limit.

examples.question: Find the sum of the series Σ_{n=1}∞ 1/(n(n+1)). Show that the series converges.
steps: Write the term with partial fractions. 1/(n(n+1)) = A/n + B/(n+1). Multiply by n(n+1): 1 = A(n+1) + B n = (A+B)n + A. So A = 1 and A+B = 0, giving B = −1. Hence 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n − 1/(n+1).
The partial sums converge to the finite number 1, so the series converges and its sum is 1.
examples.answer: The series converges to the sum 1.
examples.check:
N = 1000000
S = sum(1/(n*(n+1)) for n in range(1, N+1))
print(round(S, 10))

traps: aₙ → 0 does not prove Σaₙ converges. The harmonic series has 1/n → 0 and diverges.
The sum of a series is not the limit of its terms. It is the limit of its partial sums.
Use a/(1−r) only for a geometric series with |r| < 1. Here a is the first term, not the common ratio.
In telescoping, S_N ends at b₁ − b_{N+1}. Keeping b₁ − b_N leaves the wrong last term.
The Cauchy criterion for series looks at a whole block a_{n+1} + … + a_m, not only at one pair a_{n+1}.

quiz.q: Define the N-th partial sum and what it means for Σaₙ to converge.
quiz.a: S_N = a₁ + … + a_N. The series converges when lim S_N = S for a finite real S.

quiz.q: Explain why aₙ → 0 is not enough for convergence.
quiz.a: The harmonic series has aₙ = 1/n → 0, but its partial sums grow without bound, so it diverges. The nth term test gives only a necessary condition.
Geometric with a = 3, r = 1/4, |r| < 1. Sum a/(1 − r) = 3/(3/4) = 4.

quiz.q: If Σaₙ converges and Σbₙ diverges, prove Σ(aₙ + bₙ) diverges.
quiz.a: Suppose Σ(aₙ + bₙ) converged. Since Σaₙ converges, subtract it: Σbₙ = Σ(aₙ + bₙ) − Σaₙ would converge, contradiction.

quiz.q: State the Cauchy criterion for a series in words.
quiz.a: For every ε > 0 there is an integer N such that for all m > n ≥ N, every block of consecutive terms after index n has absolute sum less than ε: |a_{n+1} + … + a_m| < ε.

quiz.q: Show by grouping that the harmonic series diverges.
quiz.a: Group 1/3 + 1/4 ≥ 1/2, 1/5 + … + 1/8 ≥ 1/2, and so on. Each block from 1/(2^k + 1) to 1/2^{k+1} has 2^k terms, each at least 1/2^{k+1}, so block sum ≥ 1/2. Infinitely many blocks make partial sums exceed any bound.

quiz.q: Does Σ n/(n+1) converge? Use the nth term test.
quiz.a: aₙ = n/(n+1) → 1, not 0. So the series diverges by the nth term test.

beyond: Not for the exam. Numerical software adds series until the next term is below a tolerance; the error after stopping is the tail. Fourier series write a periodic signal as a sum of sines and cosines, and the same partial-sum idea controls convergence. In finance, a perpetuity is a geometric series whose sum is the present value. Search next for “tail of a series”, “p-series”, and “Fourier series convergence”.
